title: Aryadeva
hook: Nagarjuna's student, who carried the middle way on

segments.voice: Yesterday, Suhrllekha, Nagarjuna's letter of advice to a royal friend: honor it like a Buddha carved from plain wood. What did your own letter say? Day nine hundred sixty.

A great teacher is only half of a lineage. The other half is the person who listens closely enough to carry it after the teacher is gone. Nagarjuna had such a student. His name was Aryadeva, and tradition remembers him less for inventing a new idea than for taking his teacher's middle way out into the world and testing it. In debate halls, against rival schools, and in verses of his own. Today, the one who carried it on.
screen: `HALF OF A LINEAGE.` → `ARYADEVA, THE STUDENT.` → `TAKING THE MIDDLE WAY OUT.`

segments.voice: First, the eye. Tradition also calls him Kanadeva, and explains the name as the one-eyed deva, and tells a legend to account for it. Someone admired one of his eyes, so he took it out and gave it away, to show that the body is not worth clinging to. It is a legend, and it is told to make a point about letting go. Second, his book. Aryadeva wrote a work called the Four Hundred, a collection of verses that takes Nagarjuna's emptiness and puts it to work against clinging: to permanence, to the body, to pleasure, to the self. Third, a teacher's order. One verse in it lays out an order. First turn a student away from harmful actions. Then, in the middle, away from the idea of a solid self. And last, away from every view at all. Even emptiness is not a place to cling. That is a teacher thinking about how a student actually grows: one step, then the next. Fourth, a hard ending. A Chinese account of his life says a follower of a rival he had defeated in debate attacked him with a knife. As he lay dying, Aryadeva told his own students not to chase the man, and spoke of the attacker with compassion. In that telling, the last thing he taught was the teaching itself, lived. A student who carried it to the end.
screen: `KANADEVA, THE ONE-EYED.` · `THE FOUR HUNDRED VERSES.` · `HARM, THEN SELF, THEN ALL VIEWS.` · `DON'T CHASE HIM.` · then, large: `THE STUDENT CARRIES IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from a student's student. Bring to mind one thing a teacher showed you, a way of cooking, of fixing something, of calming down. Settle, and breathe. Ask how you do it now. What did you keep exactly as you were shown? What did you test for yourself, and change? Aryadeva took his teacher's way and tried it out in the world. Notice where you have done the same. Then rest with it. The bell holds the time.
Aryadeva. Nagarjuna's student, who wrote the Four Hundred verses and, in a Chinese account, forgave the man who struck him down. Today's word.
Your line: the student carries it. Today, pass on one small thing someone taught you, and if you can, say who taught it. Day nine hundred sixty.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, Aryadeva's Four Hundred verses are studied alongside Nagarjuna's works in the Madhyamaka curriculum, and teachers explain its verse on the order of teaching.

original.note: Sanskrit name of Nagarjuna's student; tradition also calls him Kanadeva.

trapdoor: what you thought: a minor name in Nagarjuna's shadow.
what it means: the student who carried the middle way into debate and verse, and in one account forgave the man who attacked him.
what a scholar hears: the Four Hundred, and its verse on the order of teaching: first turn from harm, then from a self, then from all views.
recall: the Pure Land school of Shinran

sources.ref: Catuhshataka (Four Hundred Verses) 8.15 (the order of teaching)

notes: Catuhshataka 8.15 paraphrased: first prevent non-merit, in the middle prevent the self, finally prevent all views. Confirm verse number and paraphrase.
Themes of the Four Hundred (permanence, body, pleasure, self) are a summary of its early chapters; confirm.
'Four Hundred' is the work's title (Catuhshataka); no other count is stated.

Eye legend: the Chinese Life of Aryadeva (attributed to Kumarajiva) and Tibetan sources tell different versions (offering an eye to a goddess image or to a woman/deity who admired it). Told generally as a legend; confirm the phrasing and the name Kanadeva.
Death story (stabbed by a disciple of a defeated teacher; told his students not to pursue the man) from the Chinese Life; confirm.
No birthplace or dates given (tradition places his birth in Sri Lanka) under the claims rule.
